q: A player who gets cramp during a match can be given a medical break to recover.
detail: No break is allowed for problems that were present or expected at the start of the match, or for effects such as **exhaustion or cramp resulting from the way play has gone**. Breaks of up to 10 minutes are for accidents and injuries, authorised by the referee.

q: A player may stop a rally to ask for a time-out.
detail: A time-out can only be requested **between rallies**, once the game has started, by making a T-sign.

q: Between games and during time-outs, players may go beyond the surrounds but must stay within 3 metres of the playing area.
detail: During intervals and time-outs, players must stay **within 3 metres of the playing area**, under the umpire's supervision.

q: Any side of the blade used to strike the ball must be covered with an approved rubber.
detail: A side of the blade used for striking must be covered with ordinary pimpled rubber or sandwich rubber, and in international play the covering must be **ITTF authorised**.

q: Playing clothing must not carry designs or words that are likely to cause offence.
detail: Clothing may be of any design, but **not with symbols or lettering that might cause offence** or bring the game into disrepute. The referee decides.

q: A player who accidentally hits the ball with the back of the racket hand, and then with the racket, loses the point.
detail: The racket hand below the wrist counts as striking the ball, and only a **deliberate** double hit loses the point. An accidental double touch in one stroke is a good return.

q: If a player accidentally moves the table during a rally, the rally is a let.
detail: Moving the playing surface is never a let: if it is penalised, **the opponent scores**. In practice only lifting, permanent shifting, displacement or intentional shaking is penalised; a slight knock is not.

q: The assistant umpire decides edge balls at the ends of the table.
detail: The AU decides only edge or side balls on **the side of the table nearest the AU**. The umpire decides edge balls at both ends and on the umpire's side.

q: If a player's racket touches the playing surface during a rally (without moving the table), the umpire takes no action.
detail: Only the **free hand** touching the playing surface loses the point. The racket touching the table is not an offence, unless it moves the playing surface.

q: When a service touches the net, the umpire should call “Let” immediately, without waiting to see where the ball lands.
detail: Wait until the ball **touches the correct court** before calling a let. If it misses the receiver's court, the receiver scores instead. An early call could interfere with play.

q: If the umpire notices an error in the serving order during a rally, they should let the rally finish before correcting it.
detail: If an order error is noticed during a rally, the umpire should **declare a let immediately**, not wait until the ball is out of play.

q: The ball goes out of play as soon as it leaves the playing area.
detail: The ball stays in play until the rally is decided. It does **not** go out of play just because it leaves the playing area or goes above the lights without touching them.

q: The clamps that attach the net posts to the table are part of the playing surface.
detail: The clamps are part of the **net assembly** (net, suspension, posts and clamps), not the playing surface. That matters: a return that touches the clamp and then the opponent's court is good.

q: If a player is bleeding, play must not continue until they have been treated and all traces of blood have been removed.
detail: If anyone in the playing area is bleeding, **play must not be resumed until all traces of blood have been removed**. Injuries are reported to the referee.

q: In an individual match, the player has the final say and can refuse a time-out called by their adviser.
detail: If adviser and player disagree, **the player decides in an individual match**; in a team match, the captain decides.

q: A player scores a point if the opponent stamps a foot loudly while serving.
detail: No law awards a point for stamping. Points can only be awarded for reasons in the laws. If it seems deliberate and unfair, it is dealt with as **behaviour** (warning, then penalty points).

q: If the assistant umpire calls “Fault” for an illegal service, the umpire cannot overrule it and awards the point to the receiver.
detail: The AU has the same power as the umpire on service legality, and that **decision stands**. The AU calls “Fault”; the umpire signals the point and calls the new score.

q: Either the umpire or the assistant umpire can warn a player for a service of doubtful legality.
detail: Either official may give **the one service warning** allowed in a match, for a service they are not sure is legal.

q: The score should be called as soon as practical after each rally.
detail: Call the score as soon as the rally is decided. A short delay is fine if loud applause or a ball retrieval would stop the players hearing it.

q: If a player fails to make a good return because they collide with the umpire's table, the rally is a let.
detail: Hazards that were there **at the start of the rally**, like the umpire's table or the surrounds, do not justify a let. The opponent scores.

q: In a team match, a yellow card (or yellow and red cards) a player receives carries forward to that player's later matches in the same team match.
detail: In a team match, **cards carry forward** between individual matches, though the penalty points themselves do not.

q: A player may not receive advice during the 2-minute practice period before a match.
detail: Players may receive advice **at any time except during rallies**, as long as play is not delayed. Practice is not a rally. (Advice between the end of practice and the first service is discouraged because it delays the start.)

q: The winner of the toss can only choose whether to serve or receive first.
detail: The winner may choose to **serve, receive, or start at a particular end**. The opponent then has the other choice.

q: Each player or pair may take one time-out in every game of a match.
detail: Each player or pair gets **one time-out per individual match**, not per game.

q: If the assistant umpire sees illegal advice that the umpire cannot see, the AU shows the adviser a yellow card.
detail: The AU **calls “Stop”, raises a hand and tells the umpire**, who then takes the appropriate action, such as showing the card.

q: The timekeeper stops the clock during towelling breaks.
detail: During a game the clock is stopped for significant breaks: **towelling**, the change of ends in the last game, fetching the ball from outside the playing area, and appeals.

q: A player who deliberately breaks their racket during a match may replace it with the umpire's permission.
detail: A racket may only be replaced if it is **accidentally** damaged so badly it can't be used. Deliberately breaking it is also misbehaviour (racket abuse).

q: A player may receive advice during the interval between games and during an authorised suspension of play.
detail: Advice is allowed **at any time except during rallies**, provided continuity of play is not affected.

q: If a player strikes the ball while holding the racket with both hands, the opponent scores a point.
detail: No law forbids it. The ball is struck with the racket **held in the hand**, so it is a good stroke.

q: A player may use any racket covering, as long as it shows the brand and the ITTF logo.
detail: The markings are required but **don't prove** the covering is currently authorised. Check it against the current list of authorised coverings (LARC).

q: The playing surface may be made of concrete.
detail: The playing surface **may be of any material**, as long as a standard ball dropped from 30 cm bounces about 23 cm.

q: A player must let the umpire inspect their racket before a match, but may refuse to let the opponent see it.
detail: The player must show the racket to **both the opponent and the umpire** and let them examine it.

q: An umpire can disqualify a player for grossly offensive behaviour without involving the referee.
detail: Only the **referee** can disqualify. For serious misbehaviour the umpire suspends play and reports to the referee.

q: In a team match, if the captain and the player disagree about taking a time-out, the captain decides.
detail: In a **team match the captain** has the final say; in an individual match, the player or pair.

q: In a team match, a player may receive advice from a spectator.
detail: In a team event, advice may come only from **people authorised to be at the playing area**, such as the team bench. Advice from the stands is illegal.

q: The umpire may give a warning, instead of awarding a point, for a player's first clearly illegal service in a match.
detail: The warning is only for services of **doubtful** legality. A clearly illegal service is always a fault, even the first one.

q: Once the ball has been tossed in service, the racket as well as the ball must be above the level of the playing surface.
detail: Only the **ball** must be above the playing surface and behind the end line. The racket may even start hidden, for example behind the server's back.

q: An umpire who is sure the assistant umpire wrongly called a net-cord service can overrule that call.
detail: If either official decides **the ball in service touched the net**, that decision stands and may not be overruled.

q: If a player's free hand touches the side of the table during play, the opponent scores a point.
detail: The penalty is for the free hand touching the **playing surface**, and the vertical sides of the tabletop are not part of it. (Moving the table would be different.)

q: A game is won by the first to 11 points, unless the score reaches 10-10.
detail: At 10-10 the game continues until one side leads by **2 points**.

q: In service, the ball must rise at least 16 cm after leaving the palm.
detail: The ball must be projected near vertically, without spin, and rise **at least 16 cm**.

q: The expedite system starts after 10 minutes of play in a game, unless at least 18 points have been scored.
detail: It also starts earlier if **both** players or pairs ask for it. Once in, it stays for the rest of the match.

q: A player may change to a different racket between games if the opponent agrees.
detail: A racket may only be changed if it is **accidentally damaged** so badly it can't be used. Agreement doesn't matter. Changing an undamaged racket is reported to the referee.

q: Only one service warning may be given to a player or pair in a match.
detail: After the single warning, any doubtful service by that player **or their doubles partner** is a fault.

q: In doubles, a service that lands on the centre line of the receivers' court is good.
detail: The centre line is **part of each right half-court**.

q: Players may towel down after every 6 points of a game.
detail: Towelling is allowed after **every 6 points** from the start of a game and at the change of ends in the last possible game.

q: An umpire may award a point against a player for any unfair action, even if no law covers it.
detail: Points may only be awarded for reasons **supported by the laws**. Unfair conduct is handled under the behaviour regulations.

q: The umpire waits for loud applause to die down before calling the score, but A serves before the call and a new rally starts.
detail: Nothing in the laws makes this rally invalid. The umpire should be ready to call promptly, but **play simply continues**; the score is called after this rally.

q: A serves with the racket in the right hand, then moves it to the left hand for the rest of the rally.
detail: A player may switch hands during play. **Whichever hand holds the racket is the racket hand.**

q: As A strikes the ball, A accidentally knocks the table and it moves very slightly. The ball lands on X's court and X makes no attempt to return it.
detail: The law says moving the playing surface loses the point, but the HMO tells umpires to penalise only **lifting, permanent shifting, displacement or intentional shaking**. A very slight accidental movement is ignored, so X simply failed to return a good ball.

q: As Y serves, B is looking at the score indicator. Surprised, B tries to return the ball but misses, then says they weren't ready.
detail: A let for “not ready” applies only if **the receiver makes no attempt** to strike the ball. B tried, so the service stands.

q: In game 1, Y was warned for a doubtful service. In game 3, you suspect but aren't sure that X's service is illegal. A fails to return it.
detail: The single warning covers the **whole pair** for the rest of the match. Any later doubtful service by Y **or X** is a fault.

q: A can't reach X's return, so A throws the racket at the ball. The ball hits the racket and goes back over the net onto X's court. X fails to return it.
detail: A thrown racket is not held in the hand, so the ball was **not struck**. A failed to make a return; the rally ended there.

q: A makes a good return but drops the racket. It slides across the playing surface and stops against the net-post clamp. Startled, X fails to return the ball.
detail: The racket was carried at the start of the rally, so it counts as **anything the player wears or carries**. It touched the net assembly (the clamp) while the ball was in play, so X scores.

q: Y serves, then A and X both make good returns. B catches the ball and tells the umpire that X should have served. B is wrong.
detail: There was no error in the order, so no let. B stopped the ball in play and failed to make a return: **X/Y score**.

q: A tosses the ball high, then catches it, realising it would have to be hit over the playing surface.
detail: The ball is in play from the moment it is **intentionally projected** from the palm. Catching it means A failed to make a correct service.

q: After a good return, X stumbles and drops the racket. To steady themselves, X puts the hand that had held the racket on the playing surface. A's next return misses.
detail: Once the racket is dropped, that hand is no longer carrying it, so it is a **free hand**. A free hand touching the playing surface while the ball is in play loses the point, and this happened before A's return missed.

q: The ball hits the back of A's racket hand and drops onto X's court just over the net. X makes a good return but touches the net with the racket while doing so.
detail: The racket hand below the wrist counts as striking, so **A's return was good**. X then touched the net assembly with the racket while the ball was in play.

q: A's return bounces on X's court and spins back over the net. X runs round the table and smashes the ball straight down onto A's court. A fails to return it.
detail: Once the ball has bounced on X's court, X may strike it **anywhere**, even on A's side of the net. X's return touched A's court directly, so it was good.

q: Y tries to hit the service while the ball is still rising and misses it completely. As it falls, Y hits it with the racket handle. It bounces in Y's right half-court, then on the centre line of the receivers' court.
detail: A complete miss is not a strike. Y then struck the falling ball with the **racket held in the hand** (the handle counts), and it landed in the correct half-courts: the centre line is part of each right half-court. **Good service; play on.**

q: While A's return is in the air, X's free hand touches the playing surface.
detail: A free hand touching the playing surface while the ball is in play loses the point.

q: A's otherwise good service clips the net and lands on X's court. X returns it into the net.
detail: A service that touches the net assembly and then the correct court is a **let**, whatever happens next.

q: In a rally, A's return touches the top of the net and drops onto X's court. X can't reach it.
detail: In a rally (not a service), a ball that touches the net assembly and then the opponent's court is a **good return**.

q: A's return goes round the outside of the net post, below net height, and lands on X's court. X misses it.
detail: A good return must touch the opponent's court, directly or after touching the net assembly. Going **around** the post is fine; only passing **through** the net, between net and post, or under the net loses the point.

q: X, standing close to the table, blocks A's return above X's court before it has bounced.
detail: Touching the ball while it is above or travelling towards the playing surface, before it has touched your court, is **obstruction**.

q: Y's service bounces in Y's right half-court, then lands on the centre line of the receivers' court.
detail: The centre line is part of each right half-court, so this is a **good service**. Play on.

q: Mid-rally, a towel falls off the surround into the playing area near X.
detail: A disturbance outside the players' control that could affect the rally is a **let**. Declare it immediately.

q: X catches A's service, claiming it touched the net. You didn't see whether it did, and you are not certain either way.
detail: Unless the umpire is **certain the ball did not touch the net**, they will usually agree to a let. (If certain, the point goes to the server.)

q: After Y's service and A's return, Y plays the next ball instead of X.
detail: The striking order is server, receiver, server's partner, receiver's partner. **Wrong player**: A/B score.

q: X raises a hand to show they are not ready as A tosses the ball. A serves anyway and X makes no attempt to play it.
detail: A service delivered when the receiver isn't ready is a **let**, provided the receiver doesn't try to return it.

q: A's shot clips the top edge of X's end line and drops to the floor. X can't play it.
detail: The white lines are part of the playing surface, and a ball touching the top edge **is a good return**.

q: Expedite is in operation and A is serving. The stroke counter calls “thirteen” as X makes the 13th return, and the return is good.
detail: Under expedite, if the receiver makes **13 good returns** in a rally, the receiver scores. The umpire calls “Stop”.
